paper_title: HeLM: Hierarchical Explicit Language Memory for Non-Markovian Manipulation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Recent advances in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have enabled fine manipulation capabilities, yet performing tasks that require working memory remains a key challenge. Most existing VLA architectures operate under a Markovian assumption, mapping only the current observation to an action, which leads to failure in non-Markovian environments. Inspired by the human 'inner monologue', we propose Hierarchical Explicit Language Memory (HeLM), a hierarchical VLA framework that maintains task-relevant history in explicit language through factorized event detection and event-triggered memory updates. We evaluate HeLM across 10 non-Markovian real-world tasks with 56 variants, including five newly formulated inter-episode tasks that require persistent context across task boundaries. HeLM improves intra-episode success by 12.8 percentage points over the strongest baseline and achieves 78% subtask success on compositional generalization tasks, while using up to 4.5x less memory and running 2.5x faster than the keyframe baseline at long horizons.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: The rise of Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models has revolutionized robotic control by enabling generalization across diverse language instructions and embodiments [1, 2]. Built on large-scale pretrained vision-language models, VLA models generate robot actions based on visual observations and natural language instructions. This approach has led to widespread deployment, with variants focusing on visual grounding [3, 4], complex reasoning capabilities [5, 6, 7], or subtask planning [8]. While recent advancements in robot policies have enhanced fine manipulation capabilities, tasks requiring working memory remain key challenge for real-world deployment. When wiping the window, the robot cannot determine whether the surface has already been wiped and ends up wiping the same area repeatedly. Such tasks are fundamentally non-Markovian, meaning that the current observation alone is insufficient to determine the optimal action. Yet most existing VLA architectures operate under Markovian assumption, treating manipulation as sequence of independent decisions. These structural limitations cause failure in memory-intensive tasks (see Fig. 1). Recently, various approaches have been proposed to address such limitations [9]. One line of work extracts latent embeddings from historical observations [10, 11] or compresses tokens into memory module [12]. While these approaches are effective to some extent, relying on latent representations makes it difficult to identify causes of failure due to limited interpretability. Another line of work directly leverages visual history by stacking past frames [13] or using keyframe annotations [14]. drawback of these approaches is computational overhead caused by accumulating image tokens, which limits long-horizon scalability. Correspondence to: kgh011016@snu.ac.kr. Other authors: {dhkim, mschoi, sylee}@islab.snu.ac.kr. Figure 1: Example of non-Markovian task. Due to architectural limitation, vanilla VLA loses track after pressing the red button and presses it again. HeLM successfully executes the task by storing progress in language memory, allowing the HLP to guide the LLP correctly. To overcome these limitations, we draw inspiration from how humans utilize an inner monologue. Just as humans manage complex tasks by internally keeping track of their progress (e.g., pressed the button twice; one more to go) or spatial data (e.g., The cup was originally on the left), we suggest that natural language can serve as an efficient and interpretable representation for robotic memory. By nature, this compact form preserves critical information (e.g., counts, locations) across long-horizon tasks. More fundamentally, language is natural memory representation for VLMbased policies: it is the native modality of vision-language reasoning, scales compactly across long horizons, and exposes inspectable memory states for analysis. Building on this insight, we propose Hierarchical Explicit Language Memory (HeLM), which incorporates language memory into robotic manipulation. HeLM separates high-level memory management from low-level action generation. Specifically, VLM-based high-level policy (HLP) maintains the task relevant history in language form and generates action commands, while VLA-based low-level policy (LLP) executes actions. Memory updates are event-triggered and occur only after task-relevant events or instruction changes. The language memory is organized into working and episodic fields according to whether information is needed within or across instructions. Together, these design choices support non-Markovian reasoning both within and across episodes. We evaluate HeLM on diverse non-Markovian tasks, including newly formulated inter-episode tasks. HeLM improves intra-episode subtask success by 12.8 percentage points over the strongest baseline and achieves 78% on compositional HLP generalization tasks. As task length grows, HeLM uses up to 4.5 less memory and runs 2.5 faster than the visual-memory baseline at long horizons. Contributions. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: We propose HeLM, hierarchical framework that maintains task-relevant history in explicit language through factorized event detection and event-triggered memory updates. Across 10 real-world tasks, HeLM outperforms memory-augmented and visual memory baselines, supported by component-level failure analysis. We formulate inter-episode persistence as an underexplored axis of robotic memory and introduce task suite of 10 non-Markovian tasks (56 variants).

sections.title: 2.1 Memory-Augmented and Hierarchical VLA Models
sections.content: VLA models such as RT-2, OpenVLA, and π0 map current visual-language observations to robot actions [15, 1, 2, 16]. Recent works extend these models with richer reasoning capabilities [17, 18, 19, 20], while hierarchical VLA frameworks decompose complex tasks into high-level instructions executed by low-level policies [8]. However, these approaches do not necessarily maintain explicit task-relevant history over long horizons. Prior memory-augmented policies retrieve latent features or historical tokens [12, 21, 22, 23, 10], while others preserve visual history through feature traces or multi-frame observations [3, 24, 25, 26, 14]. These representations can retain historical information, but provide limited access to the explicit task state required for counting, sequencing, or cross-episode recall. Language has also been used to support temporal reasoning. Inner Monologue [7] provides language feedback such as success signals and scene descriptions to support closed-loop replanning, whereas HeLM explicitly keeps task-relevant history in language over the sequence. MEM [27] combines short-horizon visual context with long-horizon textual memory, whereas HeLM separates event detection from memory updates, updating language memory only when task-relevant events are detected or instructions change. HeLM further evaluates inter-episode tasks, where completing later instruction requires information acquired during an earlier episode. RoboMemory [28] stores and retrieves past experience to support future interactions, whereas HeLM focuses on maintaining task-relevant history for the current non-Markovian task. Chameleon [29] also uses two-part memory but operates over latent multimodal tokens rather than explicit language. Overall, HeLM studies explicit language memory as compact and interpretable way to carry task-relevant information over time and across instructions.

sections.title: 2.2 Non-Markovian Manipulation Tasks in Robotics
sections.content: Manipulation benchmarks such as LIBERO and RLBench evaluate episodes independently, with environment resets and no requirement to retain information across task boundaries [30, 31, 32, 33, 34]. Recent memory-focused benchmarks such as MemoryBench, LIBERO-Mem, RMBench, and RoboMME [11, 10, 35, 36] introduce historical dependencies such as object occlusion, action history, and sequential progress. However, these benchmarks primarily evaluate memory within individual task episodes. In contrast, our task suite includes inter-episode tasks, where completing later instruction requires information acquired during an earlier episode that cannot be recovered from the current observation alone.

sections.title: 3 HeLM: Hierarchical Explicit Language Memory
sections.content: HeLMs design follows single principle: language can serve as memory representation for VLAbased manipulation. This section formalizes the non-Markovian problem (Sec. 3.1), hierarchical decomposition (Sec. 3.2), structured memory (Sec. 3.3), and event-triggered inference (Sec. 3.4).

sections.title: 3.1 Problem Formulation
sections.content: In non-Markovian manipulation tasks, the current observation ot is insufficient to fully infer the true state st. Standard VLA policies model the action distribution as Π(at ot, I), implicitly assuming that ot provides sufficient state information. However, identical observations can correspond to different underlying states depending on past events: (st ot, I) = (st o0:t, I). (1) memoryless policy conditioned only on ot cannot distinguish histories that yield the same current observation but require different actions (see Fig. 1). 3 Figure 2: Overall Architecture of HeLM. The High Level Policy (HLP) integrates language memory with pretrained VLM, which switches between detect mode that monitors events and an update mode that updates these events into language memory. The Low Level Policy (LLP), pretrained VLA, executes action commands generated by the HLP. To address this gap, we introduce an explicit, structured textual memory Mt that captures taskrelevant history, reformulating the policy as Π(at ot, I, Mt).

sections.title: 3.2 Framework Overview
sections.content: HeLM decouples semantic memory management from action generation through two-level hierarchy. As shown in Fig. 2, the HLP (πHLP ), built on fine-tuned VLM, generates action commands zt while maintaining the memory Mt based on ot and I. On the other hand, the LLP (πLLP ), implemented with VLA model, maps HLP-generated commands zt and ot to robot actions at. By design, language memory captures abstract task state, while the current observation provides immediate spatial grounding at execution time.

sections.title: 3.5 Data Generation
sections.content: HeLMs explicit text memory formulates training as standard visual instruction tuning, where each sample pairs visual observation with text prompt encoding the current memory state. Training data is synthesized from short subtask episodes via TaskSpec, logical schema that can be handwritten or LLM-generated. TaskSpec is used to synthesize DETECT and UPDATE supervision from short subtask trajectories. TaskSpec specifies the valid action commands, task-relevant events, and corresponding memory updates for each task, without prescribing fixed action sequence. During inference, the HLP receives task-specific event and action vocabularies, but not the full TaskSpec or ground-truth memory transitions. Instead, it autonomously detects events and updates its language memory based on visual observations. Appendix details the data-generation pipeline, TaskSpec schema, system prompts, and training hyperparameters.

sections.title: 4 Non-Markovian Task Suite
sections.content: To evaluate non-Markovian reasoning, we formalize inter-episode setting and introduce task suite covering both intraand inter-episode challenges.

sections.title: 4.1 Extension to Inter-Episode Setting
sections.content: Extending the formulation in Section 3.1 (fixed instruction I), we now consider settings where the agent receives sequence of instructions I1, I2, ..., with episode boundaries marked by instruction changes. Each episode follows single task instruction. At an episode boundary, the robot returns to its initial pose and the within-episode history is cleared, while the episodic context is retained. We define inter-episode tasks as those where completing later instruction requires information acquired during an earlier episode that cannot be recovered from the current observation alone. 5 Figure 4: The Real-World Evaluation Suite of HeLM. sections.title: 4.2 Task Suite Design
sections.content: Our task suite consists of 10 tasks with 56 variants and covers three cognitive challenges  (Fig. 4)  : count-dependent reasoning, order-sensitive progress tracking, and object-centric recall after occlusion or displacement. We further categorize tasks by temporal dependency. Intra-episode tasks (A1A5) require tracking information within single instruction, while inter-episode tasks (E1E5) require information from an earlier instruction to complete later one. The intra-episode tasks involve remembering how many times an action has been repeated (A1), which actions have already been completed in sequence (A2), which regions of the window have been wiped (A3), which drawers have already been searched (A4), and the current stage of multi-step manipulation (A5). The inter-episode tasks require recalling previous count (E1), human-demonstrated action sequence (E2), previously wiped regions (E3), an observed object location (E4), or an objects original position (E5). Instruction templates, task variants, and subtask decompositions are provided in Appendix B.1.

sections.title: 5.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: Baselines. We compare HeLM against three baselines. First, Keyframe-HLP is variant of our HLP that stores visual keyframes of detected events instead of textual memory, isolating the effect of memory modality. Second, PCMB-π0 augments π0 with the Perceptual-Cognitive Memory Bank (PCMB) [12], which compresses and retrieves historical tokens via memory module. Finally, Naıve-π0 [2] is the base π0 model trained end-to-end, without an explicit memory mechanism. All baselines use the same π0 action backbone fine-tuned on 150-200 demonstrations per task, controlling for low-level action capacity. HeLM and Keyframe-HLP additionally share the same HLP backbone and event supervision, enabling controlled comparison of memory modality. Appendix D.1 provides implementation details of the baselines, including the PCMB adaptation. Implementation of HeLM. We use Qwen2.5-VL-7B [37] as the backbone of HLP, fine-tuned via QLoRA [38] (rank r=16) on 130k frames generated via TaskSpec. HLP runs every 10 LLP steps. All real-world experiments use 7-DoF AgileX PiPER arm with table/wrist-view RGB cameras. Evaluation Protocol. We report mean success rate per task over 1545 trials (39 variants, 5 trials each). Subtask success rate measures the fraction of required subtasks completed, while order and termination errors are tracked separately to preserve failure-mode information. Strict task success rate requires all subtasks to be completed in the correct order with proper termination and is additionally reported for the intra-episode evaluation. sections.title: 5.2 Real-World Evaluation
sections.content: Intra-Episode. On intra-episode tasks  (Fig. 5)  , HeLM substantially outperforms all baselines. HeLM achieves 85.7% average subtask success rate, compared to Keyframe-HLP (72.9%), PCMBπ0 (39.5%) and Naıve-π0 (16.7%). Under strict task success, HeLM retains 81.3%, while KeyframeHLP drops to 29.3% and both PCMB-π0 and Naıve-π0 to 0%. The small gap between subtask and strict success for HeLM indicates reliable sequencing and termination, whereas the larger drops in the baselines reflect frequent order and termination failures (Sec. 5.3). Inter-Episode. On inter-episode tasks (Tab. 1), HeLM achieves 89.2% average subtask success rate. PCMB-π0 and Naıve-π0 are excluded as they reset internal states at episode boundaries, lacking support for cross-episode context; developing dedicated inter-episode baselines remains an open direction. Keyframe-HLP degrades to 16.6% average subtask success rate as visual keyframes accumulate across instruction boundaries. In contrast, HeLMs episode context summarizes inter-episode information, enabling reliable progress tracking across instruction boundaries.

sections.title: 5.3 Failure Analysis
sections.content: Failure Categories. We categorize observed failures into four types: Low-Level Execution (LLP fails physical execution), Detection (HLPs visual event detection fails), Order (subtask order violations), and Termination (fail to stop after task completion or premature stopping). HeLM Failures. HeLMs failures are dominated by Detection (64.1%) and Low-Level (31.2%), while Order failures are rare (4.7%) and Termination is not observed. Detection failures are primarily false positives, especially for drawer-opening (A4, E4) and completion events (A3, A5); despite conservative prompting to suppress uncertain detections, these errors lead to incorrect memory updates that the framework cannot self-correct. Low-Level failures arise in contact-sensitive manipulation (e.g., A1, A5, E1), where the LLP reaches the target region but fails to physically press or complete the interaction. Baseline Failures. Keyframe-HLP shows substantial Termination (33.3%) and Detection (20.2%) failures, reflecting confusion when visual keyframes accumulate. PCMB-π0 and Naıve-π0 are dominated by Order and Termination failures across all tasks. Overall, HeLMs failures are dominated by perception and low-level execution errors, highlighting these components as key targets for improvement. detailed breakdown of failure rates across individual tasks, along with representative failure cases, is provided in Appendix C.

sections.title: 5.5 Compositional Generalization
sections.content: Compositional Generalization Experiment Setup. We evaluate compositional generalization on novel task compositions of seen subtasks. While the LLP is fine-tuned to execute specific action commands, the HLP receives no additional finetuning on the held-out variants. The evaluation varies unseen counts, longer action orders, unseen objects, and unseen compositions of previously learned subtasks. Appendix B.2 describes the design of the held-out variants used in this evaluation. Quantitative Analysis. As shown in Tab. 4, HeLM achieves 78% average subtask success rate. Keyframe-HLP achieves 65.7% but fails to detect termination in A1, A4, and A5. These results support HeLMs ability to compose learned subtasks beyond the training configurations.

sections.content: We compare textual memory against visual keyframe baseline (Keyframe-HLP) on long-horizon performance and computational efficiency. As shown in Fig. 6, HeLM maintains 100% success on A1 long as the repetition count increases to seven and remains at least 77% on A2 long as the required action sequence grows to seven subtasks. Performance remains robust as the required task history grows within the evaluated range. Computational Efficiency. HeLM is initially slower due to autoregressive text generation, but becomes 2.5 faster at long horizons as visual tokens accumulate in Keyframe-HLP (see Fig. 6). Keyframe-HLPs peak VRAM usage reaches 28 GB for an 8-event episode, while HeLM remains under 6 GB. This scaling advantage comes with additional HLP inference over plain VLA. Appendix F.2 further evaluates smaller HLP and LLP backbones and their trade-off between subtask success and inference cost.

sections.title: 6 Limitations, Future Work, and Conclusion
sections.content: Limitations and Future Work. Several limitations remain. First, HeLM relies on predefined taskrelevant events through TaskSpec, which requires task-specific event definitions and does not address open-ended discovery of what should be remembered. Second, our evaluation focuses on discrete events and does not cover continuous state tracking such as liquid levels or precise geometric history. Third, the current synchronous chunk-level HLP invocation introduces inference overhead and may miss transient events that occur entirely within an LLP action chunk. Fourth, the benefit of separating working and episodic memory, relative to using single persistent language memory, remains to be evaluated. These limitations motivate more adaptive event discovery, alternative memory organizations, and higher-frequency or asynchronous high-level inference. Conclusion. We introduced HeLM (Hierarchical Explicit Language Memory) for non-Markovian manipulation, where current observations alone are insufficient for action selection. HeLM maintains task-relevant history in explicit language and decouples high-level memory management from low-level action generation. Across intraand inter-episode tasks, HeLM improves long-horizon progress tracking and enables information from earlier interactions to guide later decisions. These results highlight memory representation as an important design dimension for robot policies and show that language provides compact and interpretable interface for maintaining task-relevant history over time.

sections.title: A HeLM Implementation
sections.content: This section provides implementation details of HeLM including: dataset generation method using taskspec, system prompt for two modes of HeLM HLP, and train hyperparameters. Train Dataset Generation. To train the HLP model with robust event-driven reasoning, we developed TaskSpec-driven data generation pipeline. This approach leverages key architectural advantage of HeLM: unlike latent memory models [12, 10] that require full video histories for training, HeLMs explicit text memory decouples the current decision from the raw visual past. This allows us to treat each training sample as an independent tuple of observation and memory state ot, Mt. We define TaskSpec as schema that maps specific stages of nonMarkovian tasks (e.g., count: 2) to corresponding event frames and valid memory states. As in Fig 12, TaskSpec explicitly specifies the valid action commands, detected events, and corresponding memory updates at each stage, ensuring consistent alignment between visual observations and language memory states. Using this schema, we synthetically generate dataset without manually collecting data for every task variant. Figure 7: Generation of HeLM data. Instead of recording multiple episodes of long-horizon non-Markovian tasks, we use task configuration list to logically stitch together short subtask episodes. By sampling image frames from raw episodes and pairing them with language memories defined in TaskSpec, we create massive variations of logic-intensive scenarios. This effectively teaches the model to handle language memory; intra-episode sequential logic (updating mwork) and inter-episode context transitions (promoting mwork to mepi) by exposing it to diverse language memory-visual observation combinations. Crucially, events act as discrete anchors that trigger memory updates, allowing the model to learn when and how memory should change based on visual evidence rather than continuous observation streams. TaskSpec Generation. TaskSpec authoring involves defining the logical schema (event vocabulary, action commands, memory transition rules) per task. Task variants are generated by GPT using the hand-written TaskSpec as template, with manual verification for schema consistency  (Fig. 13)  . The main manual cost is event frame annotation, approximately 5 minutes per subtask (covering 30 episodes). 15 Table 5: Training hyperparameters used for HeLM. We fine-tune Qwen2.5-VL (7B) as the HLP for our model.

sections.title: C Failure Analysis
sections.content: We analyze failure cases of HeLM and baselines on both intra-episode and inter-episode tasks. We categorize failures into four types as shown in Fig. 8: (i) Low-Level Failure: The agent produces actions aligned with the action command but fails to physically achieve the intended outcome. (ii) Detection Failure: Incorrect event deincluding false positives and false tection, negatives. This category applies only to event-detection-based methods (HeLM and Keyframe-HLP). (iii) Order Failure: The agent fails to follow the required subtask order in order-sensitive tasks. (iv) Termination Failure: The agent fails to stop after task completion and continues executing actions. Figure 8: Four Types of Failure Cases. Examples of low-level, detection, order, and termination failures. Failure Analysis. Tab. 7 shows that HeLMs failures across intra-episode tasks (A1A5) are dominated by detection failures (9.1% of trials) and low-level failures (4.4%), while order violations are rare (0.7%) and termination failures are not observed. Among HeLMs failure cases, detection and low-level errors together account for the majority of failure types. Qualitatively, HeLM rarely fails in short-horizon intra-episode tasks such as A1 and A3, indicating that its reasoning and memory are generally stable within an episode. When failures occur, they concentrate in two cases. Low-level failures mainly arise in contact-sensitive manipulation, where the high-level reasoning is correct but the low-level policy does not produce the precise action. Detection failures are primarily false positives, especially for drawer-opening (A4) and completion (A3, A5) events. In A4 and E4, the dominant failure case is detecting the drawer as opened even when it has not been opened. This distinction is important for recovery: while repeated execution attempts can eventually resolve low-level failures when no progress event is detected, false-positive detections lead to incorrect next action commands. Overall, these results suggest that HeLMs remaining bottlenecks are (i) contact-accurate low-level execution and (ii) robust event detection under occlusion. As summarized in Tab. 7, Keyframe-HLP exhibits substantially higher overall failure rate, with termination failures (33.3%) and detection failures (20.2%) as the dominant categories, along with order failures (4.6%) and low-level failures (2.2%). We also observe incorrect event detection (before task completion) in tasks such as A3, where completion is detected from an early keyframe. These issues become more severe in inter-episode settings, where the method frequently fails to terminate or to maintain progress memory consistently across episodes. For π0-based baselines (PCMB-π0 and Naıve-π0), failures are dominated by termination and order failures, while detection failures are not applicable as these methods do not explicitly detect events. Qualitatively, they frequently generate action streams with weak global structure: order-sensitive tasks (e.g., Press in Order) are often violated, and stopping conditions are unreliable. PCMBπ0 occasionally exhibits weak local ordering (recurring short action-to-action patterns), which can yield sporadic partial progress, but this remains insufficient for robust long-horizon sequencing and termination. Conclusion of Failure Analysis. Taken together, these analyses indicate that HeLM not only achieves the highest overall success rate, but also exhibits fundamentally different failure profile from the baselines. In particular, failures in HeLM rarely originate from language memory management at the high level. Instead, the dominant failure sources can be attributed to limitations of the underlying models: detection failures from the VLM and contact-sensitive execution failures from the VLA. This suggests that performance gains are likely to come from improving visual event detection and low-level control models rather than the memory mechanism itself. In contrast, Keyframe-HLP suffers from frequent failures in interpreting multiple visual observations as coherent memory states, leading not only to detection errors but also to progress-tracking and termination failures. Similarly, π0-based baselines (PCMB-π0 and Naıve-π0) exhibit pervasive order and termination errors across nearly all tasks, reflecting the lack of explicit memory structure for long-horizon reasoning. These comparisons highlight that HeLMs explicit language memory is critical factor for stable sequencing and termination, and that its remaining limitations stem primarily from perception and execution rather than memory reasoning itself.

sections.title: D Experiment Details
sections.content: In this section, we introduce the baselines and provide detailed description of the evaluation metric. 20 D.1 Baselines We compare HeLM against three representative baselines to evaluate the impact of explicit language memory on non-Markovian task performance. First, Keyframe-HLP serves as direct comparative variant that maintains visual keyframes of detected events instead of converting them into textual memory. Second, Naıve-π0 is included as fundamental memoryless baseline that maps observations directly to actions without any historical reasoning mechanism. Finally, PCMB-π0 adapts the latent-memory bottleneck mechanism of the 7B-parameter MemoryVLA [12] to the more computationally efficient π0 backbone, as the original models scale poses significant challenges for fine-tuning under limited GPU resources. Keyframe-HLP: We implement the visual keyframe memory baseline by adapting the hierarchical architecture of HeLM. The original HeLM framework operates in two stages: the detect mode HLP identifies the event frame, and the update mode HLP updates the memory based on the event. For our baseline, we modify the memory modality: instead of language memory, we store the raw RGB frame as keyframe memory and stack them sequentially. We retain the same event detection logic to isolate the effect of memory modality. Consequently, the policy receives sequence of historical keyframes ([Ie1 , Ie2, . . . , Icurr]) as input, enabling direct comparison between visual and language memory representations. Naıve-π0. As strong VLA baseline, we employ π0 [2], flow-matching-based policy that maps visual observations and language instructions directly to continuous action trajectories. The model is trained end-to-end without any explicit memory mechanism, conditioning each action prediction only on the current observation and task instruction. To ensure fair comparison with HeLMs LLP, we fine-tune π0 on the same per-task demonstration set (150-200 demonstrations per task) using identical training hyperparameters. The model takes the current RGB observation and language instruction as input and outputs an action chunk of horizon = 10. PCMB-π0. We adapt the Perceptual-Cognitive Memory Bank (PCMB) mechanism of MemoryVLA [12] to the π0 backbone, since the original 7B-parameter model poses significant challenges for fine-tuning under our compute budget. The PCMB module compresses high-dimensional visual observations into compact latent memory bank (Dlow = 512), retaining only semantically relevant features for downstream action prediction. Our implementation preserves the core PCMB mechanism: (i) persistent memory bank that aggregates historical visual tokens, (ii) time-aware learnable cross-attention mechanism with sinusoidal time embeddings to resolve perceptual aliasing between similar observations at different timesteps, and (iii) soft update rule with rate β = 0.01 to enable gradual memory consolidation rather than abrupt overwrites. We adapt three aspects to the π0 backbone. First, we set the memory slot capacity to = 16, determined empirically to balance memory capacity and computational overhead. Second, to synchronize memory updates with π0s chunked action generation (H = 10), we implement action-horizon aligned training, where memory states are updated in tandem with action chunks rather than at every timestep. Third, we fine-tune the resulting model on the same per-task demonstration set as HeLMs LLP (150-200 demonstrations per task) under identical training hyperparameters. We note that scale differences between the original 7B MemoryVLA and our π0-based adaptation may affect performance characteristics. Our adaptation isolates the PCMB mechanism for fair comparison under the same backbone and training budget as other π0-based baselines. Limitations of Naıve-π0 and PCMB-π0. We identify two architectural limitations of these baselines that affect their performance on our task suite. 21 Termination behavior. Neither model exhibits explicit termination behavior. The flow-matching objective is designed to model continuous action distributions rather than discrete stopping events, leading to two common failure modes: (i) the model continues executing actions after task completion, and (ii) the model produces ambiguous low-velocity actions that neither stop nor advance the task. While termination tokens could in principle be added through additional supervision, this would require modifying the underlying π0 training pipeline beyond the scope of fair baseline comparison. Inter-episode capability. Inter-episode tasks pose fundamental challenge for these architectures. Since the policy distribution is strictly conditioned on the current tasks language instruction, latent features or memory bank states formed under previous tasks instruction become contextually irrelevant once that task concludes. These models lack mechanism to leverage historical observations from completed task when transitioning to new task where no explicit command exists to retrieve past context. We explored simple workarounds to extend these baselines to inter-episode settings, including (i) concatenating previous and current task instructions as single extended prompt, and (ii) providing the final observation of the previous episode as additional input context. In preliminary experiments, neither approach produced meaningful inter-episode behaviorthe models generated noisy, unstructured action sequences with no evidence of cross-episode reasoning. This empirical finding supports our methodological choice: principled inter-episode baselines require architectural modifications beyond simple context injection. For these reasons, PCMB-π0 and Naıve-π0 are excluded from the inter-episode comparison in the main paper.

Each task variant is evaluated over 5 trials, yielding 15-45 total trials per task depending on the number of variants. In our non-Markovian task suite, two additional behavioral properties are important: whether the agent follows the required subtask order, and whether it terminates appropriately after completing the task. Although these properties are crucial for long-horizon manipulation, we do not incorporate them into the numeric success rate. Instead, we record them as separate diagnostic indicators reported alongside the success rate, enabling fine-grained failure mode analysis across methods. We additionally report strict task success rate in Sec. E.1, where trial is counted as successful only if all subtasks are completed in the correct order with proper termination. For example, in task A2 (Press in Order), the instruction is to press the R, G, and buttons sequentially, which corresponds to three subtasks: {press R, press G, press B}. If the executed sequence is R, R, B, then two of the three required subtasks are achieved, yielding partial score of 2/3. In this case, we additionally mark that the required order was not followed (since was skipped), and separately check whether the agent terminated correctly. For inter-episode tasks, each instructions subtasks are counted independently. For example, E1 (Press the blue button 3 times Press the blue button 6 times total) consists of 3 subtasks in the first episode (3 presses) and 3 subtasks in the second episode (3 additional presses), yielding 6 total subtasks. The agent must correctly identify how many additional presses are needed based on memory of the first episode. 22 By reporting subtask success rates together with these diagnostic indicators, our evaluation provides quantitative measure of task progress while enabling fine-grained diagnosis of failure modes in non-Markovian tasks. sections.title: F Additional Experiments
sections.content: This section presents additional experimental analyses examining (i) HeLMs scalability to longer task sequences, and (ii) the frameworks compatibility with smaller, more efficient backbone models. These analyses highlight trade-offs between reliability, latency, and resource efficiency. F.1 Long-Horizon Robustness. We evaluate HeLMs scalability to longer task sequences using extended variants of A1 (Press Times) and A2 (Press in Order). As shown in Table 9, HeLM maintains success rates above 80% even at task length 7 on both tasks (A1: 100%, A2: 88%), demonstrating that explicit language memory remains stable as task complexity increases. This robustness stems from HeLMs compression of historical context into discrete textual tokens rather than accumulating high-dimensional visual features. By filtering out background variation and capturing only semantically meaningful events, the memory representation avoids the overhead and noise associated with raw observation history in long-horizon settings. 23 Table 9: Success rates across task lengths. We evaluate HeLM on extended variants of A1 (Press Times) and A2 (Press in Order). Task length denotes the number of required subtasks. Entries report success rates (%). The baseline configuration consists of Qwen2.5-VL (7B) as the HLP and π0 (3.5B) as the LLP, while the efficient variant utilizes SmolVLM (500M) and SmolVLA (450M). Method A1 A2 A3 A4 Avg. HeLM (base) HeLM (Smol) 100 88.8 92.2 70.4 96.6 66.6 66.6 41. 73.3 25.9 85.7 58.7 F.2 Model Generalizability and Scalability. We evaluate HeLMs compatibility with smaller backbone models by replacing the high-capacity models with significantly more efficient alternatives. The base HeLM uses Qwen2.5-VL (7B) as the High-Level Policy (HLP) and π0 (3.5B) as the Low-Level Policy (LLP). In the efficient variant, these are replaced with SmolVLM (500M) [39] and SmolVLA (450M) [40], respectively. As shown in Table 10, this transition results in reduction in the average success rate from 85.7% to 58.7%, but yields substantial improvement in computational efficiency. Specifically, the peak VRAM consumption is reduced from 13.18 GB to 2.3 GB, and the average end-to-end latency is shortened from 1.9s to 0.7s. These results indicate that HeLM can be deployed on resourceconstrained edge devices, at the cost of predictable performance trade-off. Detailed error analysis reveals that the performance degradation is primarily concentrated in the logical updates of the HLP. The reduced parameter scale of the 500M model leads to frequent failures during the UPDATE mode, including generating invalid YAML formats or updating multiple state variables simultaneously, which causes the agent to skip critical subtasks. This tendency is particularly evident in complex scenarios such as A4 and A5, where the increased length of global instructions and subtasks (see Tab. 6) hinders the construction of accurate language memory. Nevertheless, the frameworks core memory mechanismmaintaining and updating language memory across subtasksremains functional even at this reduced scale, suggesting that optimizing the memory representation into more concise and structured formats could recover success rates while preserving resource efficiency. F.3 Simulation Evaluation on LIBERO-Mem As complement to our main real-robot experiments, we ran HeLM on the LIBERO-Mem benchmark [10] to compare with published memory-augmented baselines under simulation. Benchmark Overview. LIBERO-Mem consists of 10 simulation tasks designed to evaluate four dimensions of object-centric memory: Object Motion (OM), Object Sequence (OS), Object Relations (OR), and Object Occlusion (OO). T1 and T2 (OM) test recall of the last actionsince visually identical states correspond to different required actions (e.g., lifting vs placing), the agent must remember its most recent action. T3T6 (OM + OS) extend this with repeated pick-and-place actions (3, 3, 5, and 7 times respectively); the agent must track how many times each object has been manipulated since visual cues alone are insufficient. T7 and T8 (OM + OR) test relational tracking 24 Table 11: Results on LIBERO-Mem benchmark. Top: baseline results from [10]. Bottom: our additional evaluation with π0.5 baseline and HeLM. T9 and T10 (OM + OO) test object occlusion by requiring the agent to place target object into one of two visually identical baskets and then manipulate the correct basket; the intended occlusion forces the agent to remember which basket contains the target. Benchmark Limitations. We observed two issues during evaluation that may affect interpretation of the results: (i) For T9 and T10, the wrist-mounted camera observes the baskets interior even after the target object is placed inside, so the intended occlusion does not effectively take place. This allows memoryless policies to verify object location visually rather than relying on memory, which likely explains why π0.5 alone achieves high performance on these tasks (8590%). (ii) Certain initial state configurations exhibit object spawn errorsfor instance, demos 108 and 115 spawn bottle pre-placed on its target plate, conflicting with the BDDL goal state and causing systematic failure across multiple tasks regardless of method. These environment-side issues affect all evaluated methods (memoryless baselines and HeLM) equally and are independent of method design. We therefore interpret these results as complementary simulation evidence, taking the observed benchmark limitations into account. Setup. We use π0.5 as the LLP and Qwen2.5-VL-7B as the HLP. Both the vanilla π0.5 baseline and the HeLM LLP are trained on 100 demonstrations per task under multitask training regime, following the train/validation split provided by the LIBERO-Mem benchmark (100 training + 20 validation trajectories per task). The LLP is fully fine-tuned starting from LIBERO-pretrained π0.5 checkpoint (40k55k training steps, effective batch size 24, cosine LR schedule with peak 2.5105), and the HLP is fine-tuned with QLoRA (rank 16, effective batch size 32). HeLMs LLP training data is generated by rule-based pipeline that performs subtask splitting, event annotation, and TaskSpec generation on the demonstrations, following the same procedure used for our realrobot experiments. All training is performed on 2NVIDIA A100 GPUs. Evaluation is performed on the held-out validation set: each task is evaluated over 20 rollouts using the initial states of the validation trajectories, consistent with the original benchmark protocol. We chose π0.5 over π0 as the LLP because π0 failed to learn even individual subtasks under our training regimelikely due to weaker language grounding for fine-grained subtask instructions. Using π0 as the LLP would have caused HeLMs evaluation to be dominated by LLP execution failures rather than memory-related failures, preventing meaningful assessment of the memory mechanism. For the same reason, we additionally report π0.5 alone as memoryless baseline, since the original benchmark only reports results with π0. 25 Results. As shown in Tab. 11, HeLM achieves 58.5% average success rate across the 10 LIBEROMem tasks, substantially outperforming the memoryless π0.5 baseline (36.5%) and published memory-augmented baselines (Naive E-SlotSSM: 14.8%). The improvement is most pronounced on memory-intensive tasks (T3T8), where memoryless baselines fail to reason over temporal dependencies. Discussion. The per-task pattern reveals how language memory contributes across different memory dimensions. Object Motion (T1T2). These short-horizon tasks involve minimal memory requirements (recall of the last action). HeLM outperforms π0.5 on T1 (75% vs 50%), while π0.5 performs better on T2 (80% vs 60%), reflecting that the gap between methods varies on tasks where memory plays limited role. Object Sequence (T3T6). HeLM preserves past actions in language memory and uses them to drive correct sequential execution, yielding substantial gains over the memoryless π0.5 (e.g., T3: 75% vs 15%, T5: 65% vs 15%). As the required repetition count grows (3 to 7 times), success rate decreases overall (T3: 75%, T6: 25%) due to accumulated LLP execution failures over longer horizons, even when the HLPs memory reasoning remains correct. This pattern is consistent with our main papers observation that perception and executionrather than memory reasoningbecome the dominant bottleneck as horizons extend. Object Relations (T7T8). These tasks place bowls at randomized positions and require rule-based swaps using an empty buffer plate. Each variation produces different geometric configurations, making them particularly challenging. Whether discrete language memory can preserve geometric relations is an open question for language-as-memory frameworks and question this work investigates. HeLMs success on these complex multi-step tasks (T7: 45%, T8: 10%) suggests that language memory, combined with the current visual observation, can partially preserve sufficient geometric information for relational reasoningeven without storing explicit positional encodings. Object Occlusion (T9T10). As noted in the benchmark limitations, the wrist camera circumvents the intended occlusion in these tasks, effectively reducing them to memoryless settings. Both π0.5 and HeLM achieve high performance (8590%), with the agreement between the two methods reflecting the LLPs underlying execution capability when memory is not the bottleneck. sections.title: TaskSpec Generation Prompt
sections.content: # Taskspec LLM Generation System Prompt Use the prompt below to make an LLM (Claude, GPT-4, etc.) generate HeLM taskspec JSON. Provide (1) task description, (2) LLP vocab, (3) event names, (4) episode-filter label format, and (5) any branch info the LLM outputs the JSON only. --- ## System Prompt You are HeLM **taskspec generator**. taskspec is JSON file defining how long-horizon task decomposes into LLP sub-tasks, what events the HLP must detect, and what memory state should hold at each step. Output ONLY single JSON object no prose, no markdown fences. ### Schema json { "<filename without .json>", 0, [<int per branch>], ["<full natural-language instruction>"], "task_id": "inter": "intra": "task_text": "episode_filters": [ [ {"tasks": "<label>"}, ... ], ... ], "llp_commands": "event_list": "event_grid": "memory_grid": "<n-sep vocab + done>", "<n-sep events + none + done>", [ [<event per step>, ...], ... ], [ [ {Action_Command, Working_Memory, Episodic_Context}, ... ], ... ] } ### Field meanings - **task_id** matches filename (without .json). - **inter** inter-episode transitions. 0 for single-episode tasks (default). - **intra** list of step counts, one per branch. Most tasks: [N] (single branch). Or-tasks (left/right etc.): [N1, N2]. - **task_text** list of natural-language phrasings. Usually one item. - **episode_filters** one outer entry per branch; each inner list has one {"tasks": "<label>"} filter per step in execution order. <label> must match the source _sub datasets tasks column **verbatim**. - **llp_commands** n-separated LLP vocab, **ending with done**. Every command the LLP can output. - **event_list** n-separated events the HLP can output. Must include done; also include none if the HLP needs to signal "no event yet". - **event_grid** per branch, ordered list of events that fire as sub-tasks complete. Length matches intra[b]. - **memory_grid** per branch, list of memory snapshots, length **intra[b] + 1** (extra final entry is the "done" state). Each snapshot: Action_Command (LLP command for this step), Working_Memory (short one-liner tracking progress + goal), Episodic_Context (cross-episode memory; "None" mid-task, summary at done). ### Hard rules 1. len(episode_filters[b]) == len(event_grid[b]) == intra[b]. 2. len(memory_grid[b]) == intra[b] + 1 (the +1 is the final "done" entry). 3. **Last memory_grid entry**: Action_Command="done", Working_Memory="task done (None)", Episodic_Context is short past-tense summary (e.g. "Previous_Progress: green, blue, red"). 4. Every Action_Command value must appear in llp_commands. 5. Every event in event_grid must appear in event_list. 6. **Do NOT** put none in event_grid it only lives in event_list as valid mid-execution HLP output. 7. episode_filters[b][i]["tasks"] uses the EXACT format of the source dataset: LIBERO-Mem _sub uses Python list repr ("[lift_bowl]"), free-form tasks use raw text ("press the green button"). 8. Working_Memory at step reflects state **after** step i-1s event fires (or initial state for step 0). Be consistent across steps. ### Working_Memory templates Task family Template ------ sequential (press in order) Progress: <done items> (Goal: <full sequence>) cyclic (repeat times) Count: <i> (Goal: <N>) (add , holding mid-cycle) pick-and-place with branching <Item>: <location>; Target: <next step> final step task done (None) ### Multi-branch (Or) tasks When the trajectory depends on runtime cue (cheese-on-left vs cheese-on-right, etc.), provide one entry per branch in intra, episode_filters, event_grid, memory_grid. Vocab (llp_commands, event_list) is shared across branches. --- 30 ## Worked example: press_GBR.json **Input** Task: "press the green, blue, red buttons in order". LLP vocab: press the green button, press the blue button, press the red button. Events: green button pressed, blue button pressed, red button pressed. json { "task_id": "press_GBR", "inter": 0, "intra": [3], "task_text": ["press the green, blue, red buttons in order"], "episode_filters": [ [ ] {"tasks": "press the green button"}, {"tasks": "press the blue button"}, {"tasks": "press the red button"} ], "llp_commands": "press the blue buttonnpress the green buttonnpress the red buttonndone", "event_list": "event_grid": [ "blue button pressedngreen button pressednred button pressedndone", ["green button pressed", "blue button pressed", "red button pressed"] ], "memory_grid": [ [ {"Action_Command": "press the green button", "Working_Memory": "Progress: none (Goal: green, blue, red)", "Episodic_Context": "None"}, {"Action_Command": "press the blue button", "Working_Memory": "Progress: green (Goal: green, blue, red)", "Episodic_Context": "None"}, {"Action_Command": "press the red button", "Working_Memory": "Progress: green, blue (Goal: green, blue, red)", "Episodic_Context": "None"}, {"Action_Command": "done", "Working_Memory": "task done (None)", "Episodic_Context": "Previous_Progress: green, blue, red"} ] ] } ### Why this is correct - 1 branch, 3 sub-tasks intra=[3]. episode_filters[0] and event_grid[0] both length 3; memory_grid[0] length **4** (3 + final done). - llp_commands lists all 3 commands + done (4 lines total). - event_grid[0][i] is the event that fires when step is sub-task completes (e.g. step 0 = green button press "green button pressed"). - Working_Memory updates as progress accumulates: none green green, blue task done. Each line restates the goal so context is fresh. - Final entry: Episodic_Context records the full sequence, available as memory for any downstream task. --- ## Common pitfalls - **Memory_grid length off-by-one** its intra+1, not intra. - **Vocab drift** Action_Command text not exactly in llp_commands. Copy-paste, dont paraphrase. - **Branch-count mismatch** len(intra) == len(episode_filters) == len(event_grid) == len(memory_grid). - **Filter format wrong** for LIBERO _sub, must be "[lift_bowl]" not "lift_bowl". - **none event in event_grid** never; its only an HLP output option. - **Inconsistent Working_Memory template** dont switch styles mid-task (e.g., Count: then Progress:). The prompt defines the schema, field semantics, consistency rules, and includes worked example (press GBR.json) for the press buttons in order task.
